title: Francis and the wolf
hook: Francis makes peace between the town of Gubbio and a hungry wolf (Little Flowers of St Francis 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hazelnut: Julian's vision of all that is made, small in her palm and loved. Your line was all that is made. What small thing did you hold? Day eighty-nine.

Every town has a wolf. Maybe not a real one. The neighbor everyone avoids. The kid at school who bites back. The relative who ruins every holiday dinner. The usual answer is walls, avoidance, maybe a group chat to complain in. Eight hundred years ago in Italy, a hill town called Gubbio had a real wolf, a big and hungry one, and the townspeople had stopped leaving the walls without weapons. Then a small man in a patched brown robe walked out of the gate toward it, alone, over everyone's objections. Today's story is Francis and the wolf.
screen: `EVERY TOWN HAS A WOLF.` → `GUBBIO, BEHIND ITS WALLS.` → `A SMALL MAN WALKS OUT.`

segments.voice: Francis of Assisi died in 1226, and he's one of the most loved saints in Christian history: a rich man's son who gave away everything, called the sun his brother and the moon his sister, and preached to birds. This story comes from a book called the Little Flowers of Saint Francis, a collection of tales put together in Italian more than a century after he died. So it's a story told about him, the way families tell stories about a grandparent. Here's how it goes. A fierce wolf is killing animals, and even people, around Gubbio. Francis goes out to meet it. The wolf rushes at him with open jaws. Francis makes the sign of the cross and says, come here, Brother Wolf, and tells it, in Christ's name, not to hurt him or anyone. And the wolf closes its mouth, and lies down at his feet. Now watch what Francis does. He doesn't only scold the wolf. He names what it's done, and then he names why: it was hungry. So he makes a deal with both sides. The town will feed the wolf every day, and the wolf will harm no one again. And the story says the wolf lifted its paw and put it in Francis's hand, as a pledge, right there in the town square in front of everyone. For two years after, the wolf went from door to door and was fed, and the dogs didn't even bark at it. When it died of old age, the town grieved. Brother wolf. Not a monster to kill, and not a pet either. A hungry creature, and a town that could afford to feed it. Peace asked something of everyone.
screen: `FRANCIS, WHO GAVE UP EVERYTHING.` · `COME HERE, BROTHER WOLF.` · `IT WAS HUNGRY.` · `A PAW IN HIS HAND.` · then, large: `BROTHER WOLF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed or befriend something wild. Today, maybe you'll put out water for birds, or crumbs, or simply stop and watch a squirrel or a crow without shooing it. For now, settle and breathe. Bring to mind a wild creature you've seen near where you live. Picture it clearly. Then think of your wolf: a person who bites. Without excusing anything, ask what they might be hungry for. Picture offering one small piece of it. The bell holds the time.
Francis and the wolf. The saint who walked out to meet a killer, saw that it was hungry, and made a peace that fed it. Today's word.
Your line: brother wolf. Today, when someone snaps at you, ask quietly what they're hungry for before you snap back. Day eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics and many other Christians honor Francis of Assisi as a saint of peace and of creation; on or near his feast day, October 4, many churches bless animals.

make a pact: the town feeds it, it harms no one

fork.reveal: he makes a pact with both sides: the town feeds the wolf every day, and the wolf pledges, paw in his hand, to harm no one.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint who could tame animals.
what it means: he saw the hunger behind the harm, and made a peace that asked something of both sides.
what a scholar hears: chapter 21 of the Fioretti, drawn from the earlier Latin Actus, compiled long after Francis died.

notes: Fioretti 21 paraphrased; confirm details: the sign of the cross, 'Brother Wolf', the pledge of the paw given twice (outside the gate and in the market square), two more years, dogs not barking, death of old age.
The Fioretti is a late 14th-century Italian compilation, largely from the Latin Actus beati Francisci et sociorum eius: confirm dating ('more than a century after he died').
Blessing of animals on or near October 4: common practice; confirm phrasing.
Practice suggests safe, simple ways to befriend wildlife (water, crumbs, watching); a reviewer may prefer to drop feeding given local rules.
